questions.stem: What is measured in the marble chip experiment?

options.text: The volume of gas produced in a fixed time
options.explanation: Gas volume over a set time tracks how fast the chips react with the acid.

options.text: The temperature rise of the acid
options.explanation: No thermometer reading is the measured quantity in this rate experiment.

options.text: The mass of chips dissolved after an hour
options.explanation: The method measures gas, and the window is a fixed short time.

options.text: The colour change of the solution
options.explanation: Colour watching belongs to the thiosulfate experiment.

questions.stem: Why is the measuring cylinder inverted in a water trough?

options.text: To collect and measure the volume of gas given off
options.explanation: Gas bubbles into the inverted cylinder and displaces water, so the reading gives the volume.

options.text: To keep the acid warm during the reaction
options.explanation: The trough holds water for collection, not temperature control.

options.text: To dilute the acid as it reacts
options.explanation: The acid never enters the trough.

options.text: To stop the chips from floating
options.explanation: The chips stay in the conical flask throughout.

questions.stem: How are different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate prepared?

options.text: By mixing different volumes of thiosulfate solution with water to dilute it
options.explanation: Diluting with water gives a set of strengths to compare against the acid.

options.text: By heating the thiosulfate to different temperatures
options.explanation: Heating varies temperature, not concentration.

options.text: By using different acids each time
options.explanation: The acid stays the same; the thiosulfate varies.

options.text: By adding more marble chips
options.explanation: Marble chips belong to the surface area experiment.

questions.stem: When does the stopwatch stop in the concentration experiment?

options.text: When the cross under the flask can no longer be seen from above
options.explanation: The vanishing cross is the fixed landmark that marks the same extent of clouding each run.

options.text: When the first bubbles appear
options.explanation: No bubbling landmark is used in this experiment.

options.text: After a countdown of thirty seconds
options.explanation: The endpoint is observed, not a preset time.

options.text: When the mixture turns colourless again
options.explanation: The mixture clouds and stays cloudy within the timing window.

questions.stem: Increasing the concentration of the thiosulfate has what effect on the result?

options.text: The rate increases because more particles occupy the same volume
options.explanation: A denser particle crowd collides more often, so the cross vanishes sooner.

options.text: The rate decreases because the solution is thinner
options.explanation: Dilution lowers rate; increasing concentration raises it.

options.text: The rate is unchanged because acid amount is fixed
options.explanation: The factor tested does change the rate even with fixed acid.

options.text: The rate falls to zero at high concentration
options.explanation: Nothing stops the reaction at high concentration.

questions.stem: What times the end of the temperature experiment?

options.text: The moment the magnesium strip has fully dissolved
options.explanation: The dissolving of the metal is the fixed landmark for the stopwatch.

options.text: The moment the acid starts bubbling
options.explanation: Bubbling begins almost at once, so it marks nothing useful.

options.text: A fixed countdown of one minute
options.explanation: The time is measured, not preset.

options.text: When the water bath reaches temperature
options.explanation: That happens before the reaction even starts.

questions.stem: Why does the acid sit in a water bath before the magnesium is added?

options.text: To bring the acid to a set temperature before the reaction is timed
options.explanation: The bath fixes the starting temperature so each run tests a known value.

options.text: To dilute the acid to a working concentration
options.explanation: Dilution is not the bath's job; water outside the flask never mixes in.

options.text: To keep the magnesium from reacting too slowly
options.explanation: The bath sets the temperature; it does not act on the metal directly.

options.text: To prevent the acid from evaporating
options.explanation: Evaporation is not the concern in this short experiment.

questions.stem: In the catalyst experiment, what is collected in the inverted measuring cylinder?

options.text: The oxygen produced by the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
options.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to oxygen and water, and the gas is collected.

options.text: Hydrogen given off by the catalyst
options.explanation: The catalyst does not supply hydrogen; peroxide decomposition makes oxygen.

options.text: Steam from the warm solution
options.explanation: The experiment runs at room temperature.

options.text: Air drawn in as the liquid contracts
options.explanation: Gas flows out of the flask, not air into it.

questions.stem: Why run the peroxide experiment a second time without the catalyst?

options.text: To provide a comparison that shows the catalyst's effect on the rate
options.explanation: Without the with-and-without pair, the gas volumes would prove nothing.

options.text: To use up the leftover peroxide safely
options.explanation: Safety disposal is not the experimental reason.

options.text: To double the amount of oxygen collected
options.explanation: The runs are separate measurements, not pooled samples.

options.text: To prove the catalyst is used up
options.explanation: Catalysts are not consumed, and this comparison does not test that.

questions.stem: Which factor is deliberately changed between the two peroxide runs?

options.text: The presence of the manganese(IV) oxide catalyst
options.explanation: The catalyst is the only factor the pair of runs varies.

options.text: The concentration of the peroxide
options.explanation: The peroxide stays the same so the comparison is fair.

options.text: The volume of the measuring cylinder
options.explanation: Apparatus stays fixed across the runs.

options.text: The time allowed for collection
options.explanation: The fixed time is what makes the two volumes comparable.

questions.stem: What shape distinguishes the graph of a faster reaction from a slower one?

options.text: A steeper starting gradient that becomes horizontal sooner
options.explanation: Faster reactions climb quickly and plateau early.

options.text: A shallower gradient that plateaus later
options.explanation: That describes the slower reaction.

options.text: A curve that never levels off
options.explanation: Reactions end when reactants run out, so all curves flatten.

options.text: A line that dips before rising
options.explanation: Product amount never falls in these graphs.

questions.stem: Two reactions differ only in temperature. What is true of their final product amounts?

options.text: They form the same amount of product
options.explanation: Temperature changes the pace, not the final yield fixed by the starting amounts.

options.text: The hotter one makes more product
options.explanation: The plateau is set by the reactants, not the speed.

options.text: The cooler one makes more product
options.explanation: Neither temperature wins on amount.

options.text: Neither reaction makes any product
options.explanation: Both proceed, just at different paces.

questions.stem: Which list names all four factors that can affect the rate of a reaction?

options.text: Concentration or pressure, temperature, surface area, catalyst
options.explanation: Those four are the levers named in the factor list.

options.text: Colour, temperature, surface area, catalyst
options.explanation: Colour does not change the rate.

options.text: Concentration, volume of container, light, catalyst
options.explanation: Light is not on this list, and container volume alone is not the factor.

options.text: Pressure, temperature, mass of products, catalyst
options.explanation: Product mass is an outcome, not a rate factor.

questions.stem: Why are faster rates of industrial interest?

options.text: A higher rate implies a higher rate of production and a more efficient, sustainable process
options.explanation: Faster chemistry makes more product per hour, cutting cost and waste.

options.text: Faster reactions always cost nothing to run
options.explanation: Speed has costs, such as heating or catalysts; the benefit is throughput.

options.text: Faster reactions avoid the need for reactants
options.explanation: Reactants are still consumed however fast the reaction runs.

options.text: Faster reactions are always safer
options.explanation: Safety depends on the process, not the pace alone.

questions.stem: Powdering a solid reactant instead of using one lump does what to the rate graph?

options.text: It steepens the start because more surface is exposed to the other reactant
options.explanation: Powder exposes more particles at once, so the early line climbs faster.

options.text: It lowers the final plateau
options.explanation: The same amount of product forms either way.

options.text: It has no effect because mass is unchanged
options.explanation: Mass is unchanged but the exposed area is not.

options.text: It makes the reaction endothermic
options.explanation: Energy direction is unrelated to surface area.
